content.title: Kompass Initiative: Who really waited too long?
content.lead: Critics accuse the Kompass Initiative's initiators of submitting their request too late, arguing that its text's retroactive application to the vote on the EU treaties is legally problematic. But what actually arrived very late was the Federal Council's dispatch.
content.author: Alfred Gantner

image.author: Michael Stahl / NZZ
image.caption: A majority of the cantons is required for votes on the EU treaties. The Compass initiative wants to demand this, if necessary, retroactively.
image.altText: The cantonal coats of arms in the «entrance hall» of the Federal Parliament Building. Federal Parliament Building dome.

content.caption: A majority of the cantons is required for votes on the EU treaties. The Compass initiative wants to demand this, if necessary, retroactively.
content.author: Michael Stahl / NZZ

content.text: In the debate surrounding the Kompass Initiative, critics have raised an accusation that cannot go unchallenged: that Kompass/Europa submitted the initiative too late, ensuring the popular vote could not occur before the ratification of the EU treaty package. This, however, is factually incorrect. It also distracts from an uncomfortable question: What has the Federal Council itself done in the past 12 months?

The Kompass Initiative's central goal is for a double majority of the people and cantons to apply to the vote on new agreements with the EU, its initiators state. The Federal Council, however, wants the vote to proceed with a simple popular majority. In this case, a retroactive clause in the text of the Kompass Initiative demands that the ballot on the EU treaties be annulled if accepted.
These are the reasons why proponents of the EU treaties and the Federal Council complain that the Kompass Initiative was simply submitted too late.

The decision to launch the Kompass Initiative was made in winter 2023, after the Common Understanding between the EU and Switzerland became known. Official negotiations with the EU began on March 18, 2024. On Oct. 1, 2024, signature collection for the initiative started. The substantive conclusion of negotiations only followed on Dec. 20, 2024, two and a half months after collection began. Even then, only fact sheets were published, not the full treaty texts.

The unsatisfactory negotiation result — 1,889 pages of treaty text — was only published on June 13, 2025. Three months later, 140,347 signatures had been collected, and the initiative was submitted. Eleven of the legally available 18 months were needed for collection and submission — six months before the signing in Brussels and three months before the consultation report. Kompass/Europa acted as soon as it was factually justifiable and at a pace exceptional for a popular initiative.

What actually took a long time, however, was the Federal Council's dispatch to parliament. It was adopted on Aug. 12, 2026 — 17 days before the expiry of the statutory annual deadline. The Federal Council allowed nine months to pass. Had the dispatch been submitted earlier, parliament would have had the opportunity to deliberate on the initiative quickly.

This exhaustion of the statutory maximum period is not politically neutral. It significantly reduces parliamentary leeway and makes a vote on the constitutional fundamental question of the required double majority more difficult before the vote on the EU package. This represents obvious political calculation.

And this is precisely where it becomes grotesque: Federal Councillor Jans warns of the legal uncertainty that would arise if the Kompass Initiative were accepted after a vote on the EU package. But it is precisely he who, by delaying the dispatch, prevents the people from creating clarity in time. He significantly contributed to the uncertainty he warns against through his own delaying tactics.
The Kompass Initiative was not too late. It is too late to answer the fundamental question of the cantonal majority in institutional integration only after its first major application.
Alfred Gantner is a co-founder of Partners Group and a co-initiator of the Kompass Initiative.

newestTopComments.text: In a state governed by the rule of law, the administration must adhere to the constitution. Article 121a of the Federal Constitution was adopted by the people because they wanted to limit immigration. This is clearly evident from the legislative materials. It is therefore hardly comprehensible that our representatives in Brussels negotiated a solution that aims to facilitate immigration. Given this situation, Article 121a should at least be removed from the constitution. This requires a majority vote in the cantons anyway. Even complex legal opinions (such as that of Astrid Epiney) cannot change this.

Regardless of one's stance on the cantonal majority and the EU question, in a democracy, initiatives should be handled with due diligence and not obstructed. Anything else is undemocratic. And that brings us to the crucial point: How democratic is Switzerland really? A similar question could be asked regarding individual taxation. In both cases, the Federal Council and Parliament are aware of pending initiatives that could overturn recent popular votes. Instead of taking the concerns of their unpopular opponents seriously through a democratic process, a proposal is ruthlessly pushed through. Then, the initiators of the original, competing idea are accused of coercion. Wonderful. That's my idea of ​​a functioning democracy.

metadata.nzzSummaryEN:
- The Kompass Initiative demands a double majority for votes on EU agreements and proposes a potential retroactive clause, which is legally contested.
- Critics accuse the initiative of being submitted too late, while supporters blame delays by the Federal Council.
- The Federal Council's late message is seen as politically motivated, complicating a timely vote.
metadata.nzzSummaryDE:
- The Compass initiative calls for a double majority for votes on EU treaties and a possible retroactive clause, which is legally controversial.
 Critics accuse the initiative of having been submitted too late, while supporters cite delays at the Federal Council as the cause.
 - The Federal Council's late message is seen as politically motivated and makes a timely vote more difficult.

meta.seoTitle: Federal Council – All articles about the Swiss government | NZZ
meta.description: Four parties, seven members: The Swiss Federal Council, elected by parliament, has presented itself for decades with a stability that can seem puzzling to foreigners. Direct democracy, however, demands a balance of interests, because decisions must stand up to popular vote. Since 1959, the four largest parties (SVP, SP, FDP, CVP) have been part of the government. Here you can find all NZZ articles on the Federal Council.
